newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS-Dlr's strength may be illusory, experts say.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dlr's strength may be illusory, experts say.

text.p: Is the dollar's strength built on sand? Financial markets have accepted that a massive capital flow out of Japan has been a big factor behind the dollar's recent surge against the yen.
But this "outflow" may prove a mere illusion, Japan's monetary authority and institutional investors say.
The currency market cherishes the theory that a wide gap in interest rates between Japan and the United States means capital is pumped out of Tokyo into high-yielding U.S. bonds.
"However, if this theory ceases to function, the dollar will inevitably collapse (against the yen) at some point in the future," a senior currency trader said.
Until recently, the theory has held up, and massive sums of Japanese capital have poured into foreign assets, supporting such currencies as the dollar and the British pound.
In the year to January, Japanese life insurers boosted their foreign bond holdings 28.3 percent to 16.99 trillion yen ($134 billion).
But from February to April the capital flow appears for various reasons to have slowed to a trickle.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau, told Reuters on Friday; "The outflow (of capital from Japan) isn't really there."

Sakakibara added: "Japan turned a net capital importer for February and March as Japanese investors took profits on foreign bonds and repatriated the proceeds, while foreign capital kept flowing into Japan."
Ministry data shows Japan imported over one trillion yen ($7.9 billion) worth of long-term capital in February.
This was despite the fact that the rate differential between the benchmark bond yields of Japan and the United States widened to an eight-year high of more than 490 basis points, or 4.9 percent.

Growing concerns among Japanese and U.S. monetary authorities about the yen's weakness and rising Japanese exports are also keeping investors wary of committing to a similar magnitude of foreign bonds as last year.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has reiterated that he shares Japan's concern about the yen's recent fall, which could boost Japan's trade surplus.

A general manager at Nippon Life Insurance Co, the largest insurer in Japan, said: "Since life insurers, in general, bought significant volumes of foreign bonds last (fiscal) year, we're not very eager about fresh investment.
"Apart from that, it's not yet clear how much of a rise in net assets we can expect this year, having slashed the expected return for policy holders from 4.5 percent to 2.5 percent."
Until fiscal 1995/96, ending in March 1996, Nippon Life's net assets rose by two trillion yen ($15.8 billion) a year, part of which was earmarked for foreign bond investment.

Rikio Nagahama, chief general manager of Securities Investment, Dai-ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co, Japan's second-largest insurer, said: "We were buying foreign bonds at only a moderate pace in April, while monitoring the forex impact from continuing rises in (Japan's) current account surplus."
Fresh foreign bond purchases would be smaller in 1997/98 than last year, he added.
The dollar rose to a 56-month high of 127.16 yen on April 10 on a belief that capital outflows from Japan would keep buoying the dollar against the yen.
Traders and monetary authorities expect some capital flow, though not massive, from Japan to continue, though that may not have clear foreign exchange implications.

Sakakibara said Japanese institutional investors may gradually boost the foreign bond weighting in their portfolios, but added that a large amount of foreign bond buying by Japanese individual investors was unlikely to continue.
He said the impact of this on foreign exchange rates was hard to determine as investors may decide to hedge against the risks of holding such foreign assets.

In April, pension fund account managers at insurers and trust banks bought U.S. and European bonds, a U.S. brokerage house trader said. They would keep channelling funds to foreign bonds in their struggle to achieve better investment returns amid keen competition among pension fund managers, he added.
